# Calder Bay council approves $1.8 billion light-rail tunnel in narrow vote

## The vote

- The council voted 7-4 early Wednesday, October 21, after a nine-hour meeting.
- The $1.8 billion tunnel is the largest public works project in the city's 140-year history.
- The 3.2-mile tunnel will link Harbor Point ferry terminal to Eastgate medical district, with four underground stations.
- Travel time between the two areas would drop from 38 minutes by bus to 11 minutes by train.
- Mayor Elena Vargas made the tunnel the centerpiece of her 2024 campaign.
- Councilwoman Janet Ofori, Derek Huang, Priya Raman and Tom Kessler voted no.
- Council President Luis Moreno voted yes after the regional transit agency agreed to cap the city's share of cost overruns at 15 percent.

## How it will be paid for

- Federal government: $720 million through the Capital Investment Grants program, pending final review next spring.
- State: $400 million from a 2022 transportation bond.
- Local: $680 million, including about $500 million from a half-cent sales tax increase and fees on developers building within a quarter mile of stations.
- Voters approved the sales tax in March, 54 to 46 percent.
- Finance Director Carla Mendes estimated the sales tax will raise $62 million per year.
- The city plans to borrow against that revenue, with bonds repaid over 30 years.

## Opposition and concerns

- The Calder Bay Taxpayers Alliance, led by Mark Ellison, cited a 2019 University of Westbrook study finding large U.S. rail tunnels exceeded budgets by an average of 44 percent.
- Ellison said the 15 percent cap is "a promise, not a guarantee."
- Fremont Avenue business owners worry about years of construction; Ana Castillo lost nearly a third of her revenue during an eight-month water main project in 2021.
- The council added a $25 million fund, proposed by Councilman Ray Delgado, offering grants of up to $150,000 to affected small businesses. It passed 10-1, with Kessler voting no.

## Environmental review

- The final environmental impact statement, released in August, projects 14,000 fewer daily car trips downtown by 2040.
- It estimates a reduction of 31,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions per year at projected ridership.
- Contaminated soil from a former rail yard near the Union Street station could add up to $40 million, which is already included in the $1.8 billion estimate.

## Timeline

- Construction is scheduled to begin in mid-2027, with tunnel boring starting near Harbor Point.
- The boring machine, built in Germany, is expected to arrive in early 2028.
- Project director Samuel Okafor said the line should open in late 2031 if the federal grant is approved on schedule.
- A federal funding delay of more than six months would push opening into 2032.
- Projected ridership: 52,000 weekday riders in the first full year, rising to 78,000 by 2040.

## What comes next

- A funding agreement with the regional transit agency is expected in December.
- The agency's board votes on its share of the project November 14.
- The Taxpayers Alliance is collecting signatures for a measure requiring voter approval for city projects over $500 million.
- The group needs about 18,000 valid signatures by February 1 to qualify for the November 2027 ballot.
- Vargas said she is confident the project will survive any challenge.

# Tierra Alta firma un acuerdo de 2.300 millones de dólares para extraer litio en el salar de Quimal

## Acuerdo y empleo

El gobierno de Tierra Alta firmó un acuerdo con la australiana Southern Lithium y la estatal Recursos Andinos para extraer litio en el salar de Quimal, a 4.000 metros de altura. La inversión será de 2.300 millones de dólares en ocho años.

El gobernador Julián Ferreyra dijo que es "la inversión privada más grande de la historia de la provincia". Prometió 1.200 empleos directos en la construcción y 450 permanentes en la operación.

## Términos del acuerdo

Southern Lithium tendrá el 80 % de la sociedad y Recursos Andinos el 20 %. La provincia no aportará capital; su parte se pagará con regalías futuras.

- Regalías del 3 % sobre el valor en boca de mina, el máximo que permite la ley nacional.
- Aporte anual de 5 millones de dólares a un fondo para comunidades cercanas.
- Al menos 70 % de trabajadores residentes en la provincia.
- 50 % de insumos comprados a proveedores locales, si hay precio y calidad comparables.
- Revisión cada cinco años. La ministra Carolina Basualdo dijo que la provincia podrá renegociar su parte si el precio del litio sube mucho.

## Producción y mercado

Desde 2029, la planta producirá 40.000 toneladas anuales de carbonato de litio. Según la empresa, a precios actuales equivale a unos 600 millones de dólares por año.

El director ejecutivo Andrew Pike dijo que la mayor parte se venderá a fabricantes de baterías de Corea del Sur y Japón. Reconoció que el precio cayó cerca de un 75 % entre 2022 y 2024, pero sostuvo que la demanda de autos eléctricos lo impulsará antes de fin de la década. "No invertimos pensando en el precio de este año, sino en el de 2035", afirmó.

El carbonato se exportará por el puerto chileno de Antofagasta, a 620 kilómetros. La provincia se comprometió a pavimentar la ruta 52 con un crédito de 90 millones de dólares del BID.

## El agua

La empresa dice que su tecnología de extracción directa consume 60 % menos agua que las piletas de evaporación. Aun así, el estudio de impacto ambiental estima un consumo de 180 litros por segundo de un acuífero que abastece a tres comunidades.

La Mesa de Comunidades del Salar, que reúne 11 comunidades kollas, rechazó el acuerdo. Su vocera Rosa Cruz dijo que no hubo la consulta previa que exige el Convenio 169 de la OIT.

El gobierno dice que hubo 14 reuniones informativas entre marzo y agosto. Basualdo admitió que no todas las comunidades participaron.

El hidrólogo Martín Quiroga, de la Universidad Nacional de Tierra Alta, dijo que no hay mediciones confiables sobre la recarga del acuífero. Pidió dos años de monitoreo independiente antes de empezar la producción.

## Reacciones políticas

- La oposición pedirá la interpelación de Basualdo. El diputado Hernán Sosa calificó el acuerdo de "entrega" y criticó que el texto se publicara 48 horas antes de la firma.
- La Cámara de Comercio celebró el anuncio. Su presidenta, Lucía Vélez, dijo que puede "cambiar la economía de toda la región". La provincia tiene 9,8 % de desempleo, el más alto del norte del país.
- El intendente de Quimal, Ramón Choque, apoyó el proyecto con reservas y pidió que el 30 % de las regalías quede en los municipios de la zona.

## Próximos pasos

La Legislatura tiene 60 días para ratificar el acuerdo. El oficialismo tiene 19 de 35 bancas, por lo que en principio cuenta con los votos.

La construcción comenzaría en el primer semestre de 2027. La Mesa de Comunidades presentará un amparo federal la próxima semana para frenar el proyecto hasta que se realice la consulta. Ferreyra dijo que respetará cualquier decisión judicial y confía en que el proyecto avanzará.

# Calder Bay council approves $1.8 billion light‑rail tunnel in narrow vote

## The vote
- On October 21, council voted 7‑4 to approve the tunnel.
- Over 200 residents spoke; mayor Elena Vargas called it “the moment Calder Bay decided to grow up instead of out.”
- Council members Derek Huang, Priya Raman, Tom Kessler and Janet Ofori voted no; Ofori said it would drain money from neighborhoods without stations.
- Council President Luis Moreno and six others voted yes after a transit‑agency cap on cost‑overrun liability at 15 %.

## How it will be paid for
- Federal: $720 million pending review next spring.
- State: $400 million from a 2022 transportation bond.
- Local: $680 million total.
  - $500 million from a half‑cent sales‑tax increase approved March 54‑46.
  - $180 million from developer fees within a quarter‑mile of stations.
- Finance Director Carla Mendes said the tax will raise $62 million/year; bonds will be repaid over 30 years.

## Opposition and concerns
- Taxpayers Alliance director Mark Ellison warned tunnels average 44 % budget overruns; cited 15 % cost‑overrun cap as non‑guarantee.
- Business owner Ana Castillo feared prolonged construction loss; cited 2021 water‑main loss of one‑third revenue.
- Councilman Ray Delgado added a $25 million grant fund (up to $150 k per small business); amendment passed 10‑1.

## Environmental review
- Final EIS (August) predicts removal of 14,000 car trips/day by 2040 and reduction of 31,000 t CO₂/yr at projected ridership.
- Contaminated soil near Union Street station may add $40 million, already included in $1.8 billion estimate.

## Timeline
- Construction start: mid‑2027; tunnel boring begins near Harbor Point.
- Boring machine arrives early 2028 (built in Germany).
- Opening: late 2031 if federal grant on schedule; delayed to 2032 if grant >6 months late.
- Projected riders: 52,000 weekday in year 1, 78,000 by 2040.

## What comes next
- Council approval enables funding agreement with transit agency, expected December.
- Agency board votes on its share November 14.
- Taxpayers Alliance gathering ~18,000 signatures by Feb 1 for a ballot measure requiring voter approval for projects >$500 million (targeting Nov 2027 ballot).
- Mayor Vargas confident the project will survive any challenge, citing March vote support.
